math_questions.question: The decimal \(0.36\) can be written as the fraction \(\dfrac{x}{25}\). What is the value of \(x\)?

solution.exhibit_text:
Write the decimal as a fraction over \(100\): \(0.36=\dfrac{36}{100}\).

Divide the numerator and denominator by \(4\) to get a denominator of \(25\):

\[\dfrac{36}{100}=\dfrac{9}{25}\]

So \(x=9\).

math_questions.question:
At a bakery, \(14\) dozen rolls were used yesterday for \(120\) lunch customers. Today, there were \(180\) lunch customers. Assuming that the roll usage rate is the same for both days, which proportions can be used to determine how many dozen rolls are needed for \(180\) lunch customers?

Select the **three** correct answers.

solution.exhibit_text:
Each correct proportion keeps matching quantities in matching positions: dozens with dozens, customers with customers.

\(\dfrac{x}{14}=\dfrac{180}{120}\): today's rolls over yesterday's rolls equals today's customers over yesterday's customers. Correct.

\(\dfrac{14}{120}=\dfrac{x}{180}\): rolls per customer is the same both days. Correct.

\(\dfrac{120}{14}=\dfrac{180}{x}\): customers per dozen rolls is the same both days. Correct.

\(\dfrac{14}{180}=\dfrac{x}{120}\) and \(\dfrac{x}{120}=\dfrac{14}{180}\) pair yesterday's rolls with today's customers, so they are set up incorrectly. (All three correct proportions give \(x=21\).)

math_questions.question: A bag contains \(90\) marbles that are red, blue, or green. The ratio of red to blue marbles is \(4{:}3\), and the ratio of blue to green marbles is \(3{:}2\). If \(5\) blue marbles are removed and replaced with \(5\) green marbles, what will be the new ratio of red to green marbles?

solution.exhibit_text:
Both ratios share blue \(=3\), so red : blue : green \(=4:3:2\), which is \(9\) parts. Each part is \(90\div9=10\) marbles: \(40\) red, \(30\) blue, \(20\) green.

After the swap there are \(20+5=25\) green marbles (red is unchanged at \(40\)).

\[40:25=8:5\]

math_questions.question: At Eastview Middle School, a survey asked two questions, Question A and Question B. For each question, students could answer either "yes" or "no." Of the \(900\) students who responded to the survey, \(760\) answered "yes" to Question A, and \(610\) answered "yes" to Question B. What is the **least** possible number of these students who could have answered "yes" to **both** questions?

solution.exhibit_text:
The overlap is smallest when as many students as possible said "yes" to only one question. Adding the two "yes" groups counts the overlap twice:

\[760+610-900=470\]

At least \(470\) students must have said "yes" to both.

math_questions.question: In a sample of \(80\) cars at a local dealership, there are \(20\) red cars and \(16\) cars with sunroofs. Of the \(20\) red cars, \(6\) have sunroofs. If a car is selected at random from the given sample, what is the probability that **both** of the following are true: the car is **not** red and does **not** have a sunroof?

solution.exhibit_text:
Cars that are red **or** have a sunroof: \(20+16-6=30\) (the \(6\) red cars with sunroofs were counted twice).

\[\dfrac{50}{80}=\dfrac{5}{8}\]

ela_passages.title: The Long, Slow Life of the Deep Sea's Oldest Animals

paragraphs.text: About forty-two hundred years ago, around the time the first great cities of Mesopotamia were raising their walls of mud brick, a tiny larva of black coral drifted through the dark water off the coast of Hawaii. It was smaller than a grain of rice, little more than a speck of living jelly. It may have ridden a deep ocean current for days or even weeks, carried far from the colony that released it. Or it may have been pulled along by the slow churn of water around an undersea mountain, where currents curl and eddy like wind around a cliff. Most larvae never find a place to settle. This one, however, came to rest on a rocky ledge more than a thousand feet below the surface. Within a few days, it had fastened itself in place and begun to build a skeleton—a stub no taller than a pencil eraser, crowned with a few pale tentacles.

Most coral larvae die before they ever find a home; far fewer than one in a hundred survive their first year. The survivors are often found clinging to the remains of older colonies. The seafloor where black corals grow is scattered with fallen skeletons—branches, stumps, and crumbled pieces that broke away long ago. In the cold, still water, these remains do not dissolve quickly; instead, they wear down slowly, like stones polished by a stream. They offer young corals two things that are rare in the deep sea: a hard, clean surface to hold on to and minerals that help a new skeleton form. The young colony grows from the remains of its ancestors—a nursery built on a graveyard.

Near the sunlit surface, a branching coral such as staghorn coral can grow several inches in a single year. Black corals grow almost unbelievably slowly. After a decade, the young colony on the ledge would have been only a little taller, its single stem just beginning to split into thin branches. Its polyps are tiny, and each has six tentacles that sweep the water for drifting specks of food. A century may have passed before the colony was as tall as a child, and centuries more before it spread into the feathery, treelike shape for which black corals are known. Despite its name, the living coral is not black at all; its soft tissue is orange, yellow, or white. Only the skeleton underneath is dark. By the time the colony reached its full height of several feet, the cities of Mesopotamia had long since crumbled into dust.

Many corals live for decades, and some reefs have stood for thousands of years—though the individual animals that built them have come and gone many times. Once a black coral colony has taken hold, however, it can survive as a single living organism for an astonishingly long time. Living far below the surface, it is out of reach of the crashing waves and powerful storms that break apart shallow reefs. The water around it stays cold and dark year after year, with few sudden changes in temperature. Because so few animals can live in such a place, the colony faces little competition for space. Its skeleton, made of a tough, hornlike material, is so hard that few creatures can bore into it or break it down.

Kingdoms rose and fell, ships crossed oceans for the first time, and cities grew from villages into skyscrapers—and all the while, the coral from 2200 B.C. carried on with its patient, unhurried existence, thickening its trunk by less than the width of a human hair each year. Like a tree, a black coral adds a thin ring to its skeleton as it grows, which makes black corals an especially valuable record of conditions in the deep ocean over thousands of years. When the water warms or cools, the chemistry of the rings changes. When the ocean holds more or less of certain substances, the layers keep track of the difference.

As the centuries pass, an old black coral becomes battered and strange. Its oldest branches lose their living tissue. Pieces snap off and drift down to the seafloor. At first glance, the colony may look dead. Such is the case of one ancient colony that still hangs on to a ledge off the island of Hawaii, where research submarines sometimes pass on their dives. Bare, dark branches jut out in every direction. Much of the trunk has been stripped down to bare skeleton, like the frame of a building after a fire. A thin coat of living tissue still covers the tips of some branches, where the polyps go on catching food and sharing it with the rest of the colony. All told, the colony is not much to look at; most visitors who glimpse it through a submarine window hardly notice it at all.

No two ancient colonies look exactly alike, and the scientists who study them sometimes speak of them as if they were individuals. People have always been tempted to see themselves in long-lived creatures; black corals have been called elders, survivors, the grandparents of the sea. Warming oceans and the harvesting of black coral for jewelry have led to worried headlines about their future, although many marine scientists believe that the deepest colonies are not in immediate danger. They have outlasted ice ages and shifting seas before; they may outlast us.

questions.question: What is the effect of describing a young black coral colony as “a nursery built on a graveyard” (paragraph 2)?

options.A: It suggests that young colonies are more fragile than older colonies are.
options.B: It shows that the seafloor where black corals live is a dangerous place for young animals.
options.C: It emphasizes the young coral's ability to use what earlier generations of black coral left behind.
options.D: It reveals that black corals grow more quickly when they live close to one another.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The comparison describes where young colonies grow and what they use, not how fragile they are compared with older colonies.
B. Incorrect. Although paragraph 2 says that most larvae die, the “graveyard” image is about the remains of older colonies helping new ones, not about danger on the seafloor.
C. CORRECT. The “graveyard” is made of “the remains of its ancestors” (paragraph 2)—fallen skeletons of older black corals—which give the young colony “a hard, clean surface to hold on to and minerals that help a new skeleton form.”
D. Incorrect. Paragraph 2 says nothing about colonies growing faster when they are close together; the comparison is about using remains left by earlier generations.

questions.question: In paragraph 4, the idea that the black coral can survive for a very long time is illustrated mainly through

options.A: a description of specific qualities that make the black coral suited to its deep-sea environment.
options.B: a comparison of the black coral with shallow-water reefs that last for thousands of years.
options.C: an explanation of why the waters off Hawaii are the best place for black corals to grow.
options.D: an examination of why few other animals compete with black corals for space.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. CORRECT. Paragraph 4 lists several qualities that help the black coral survive: it lives below the reach of waves and storms, its water stays cold and steady, it faces “little competition for space,” and its skeleton is “so hard that few creatures can bore into it.”
B. Incorrect. Paragraph 4 mentions reefs that stand for thousands of years, but it points out that the animals that build them “have come and gone many times”; this contrast is not how the paragraph shows the black coral's ability to survive.
C. Incorrect. The paragraph describes conditions in the deep sea in general, not why Hawaii in particular is the best place for black corals.
D. Incorrect. The lack of competition is only one of several qualities in the paragraph, so it is not the main way the idea is illustrated.

questions.question:
Read this sentence from paragraph 5.

“Kingdoms rose and fell, ships crossed oceans for the first time, and cities grew from villages into skyscrapers—and all the while, the coral from 2200 B.C. carried on with its patient, unhurried existence, thickening its trunk by less than the width of a human hair each year.”

The sentence contributes to the development of ideas in the passage by

options.A: explaining the reason for the black coral's long life.
options.B: emphasizing that human achievements last less long than natural ones.
options.C: describing how precisely the black coral's growth can be measured.
options.D: highlighting the extremely slow pace of the black coral's life.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The sentence describes how slowly the coral lives and grows; the reasons for its long life are given in paragraph 4.
B. Incorrect. The kingdoms, ships, and cities are mentioned to show how much changed in human history while the coral barely changed, not to argue that human achievements do not last.
C. Incorrect. “Less than the width of a human hair” is a vivid comparison, but the point of the sentence is how slow the growth is, not how precisely it can be measured.
D. CORRECT. The sentence sets huge, fast-moving changes in human history (“Kingdoms rose and fell”) against the coral's “patient, unhurried existence,” which makes its extremely slow pace of life stand out.

questions.question: Which claim is best supported by the details in paragraph 5 about the rings in a black coral's skeleton?

options.A: Black corals can be used to learn about changing ocean conditions because they live for so long.
options.B: Black corals must be protected so that scientists can keep studying the deep ocean.
options.C: The rings in a black coral's skeleton allow scientists to predict future changes in the ocean.
options.D: The slow growth of black corals helps them survive changes in the temperature of the ocean.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. CORRECT. Paragraph 5 says the rings make black corals “an especially valuable record of conditions in the deep ocean over thousands of years”; because a colony lives so long, its rings record changes in temperature and chemistry across a very long span of time.
B. Incorrect. Paragraph 5 explains why the rings are valuable but does not say the corals must be protected; threats to the corals are mentioned only in paragraph 7.
C. Incorrect. The rings record conditions that have already happened (“keep track of the difference”); the paragraph does not say they can predict the future.
D. Incorrect. Paragraph 5 connects the rings to changes in temperature, but it does not say that slow growth helps the coral survive those changes.

questions.question: The phrases “still hangs on” and “stripped down to bare skeleton” in paragraph 6 are used to highlight

options.A: that the colony is in danger and needs protection in order to survive.
options.B: that the colony survives even though much of it is no longer alive.
options.C: how the colony's unusual shape attracts the attention of visitors.
options.D: how the colony can be mistaken for a different kind of animal.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The phrases suggest the colony looks worn, but nothing in paragraph 6 says it needs protection.
B. CORRECT. “Stripped down to bare skeleton” shows that much of the trunk is no longer living, while “still hangs on” emphasizes that the colony is nonetheless alive, with “a thin coat of living tissue” still catching food.
C. Incorrect. The paragraph says the opposite: “most visitors who glimpse it through a submarine window hardly notice it at all.”
D. Incorrect. The paragraph says the colony “may look dead,” not that it looks like a different animal.

questions.question: What is the best summary of the black coral's life cycle?

options.A: A black coral larva drifts through deep water until it settles on a rocky ledge. Over time, it grows thin branches and develops polyps with six tentacles that catch drifting food.
options.B: A black coral grows very slowly in a deep, steady environment where few other animals can live. Over time, its oldest branches lose their living tissue, but living tissue on other parts keeps catching food for the colony.
options.C: A black coral settles on the skeletons of older colonies and slowly grows into a treelike shape. Over time, its living tissue changes from orange or yellow to black.
options.D: A black coral lives only in the waters off Hawaii. Over time, storms break off many of its branches, but its trunk remains covered in living tissue.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. This summary focuses on minor details about settling and tentacles and leaves out the later stage in which the colony's oldest parts lose their living tissue (paragraph 6).
B. CORRECT. This summary gives the key stages in order: very slow growth in a harsh but steady deep-sea environment (paragraphs 3–4), followed by old age, when parts of the colony become bare skeleton while living tissue elsewhere keeps feeding it (paragraph 6).
C. Incorrect. The passage says the living tissue is “orange, yellow, or white” and that “only the skeleton underneath is dark”; the tissue does not turn black.
D. Incorrect. Black corals do not live only off Hawaii, storms do not reach them (paragraph 4), and much of the old colony's trunk is bare skeleton, not living tissue (paragraph 6).

questions.question: Throughout the passage, the author conveys a point of view mainly by

options.A: comparing the black coral to ancient kingdoms that rose and fell over thousands of years.
options.B: arguing that black corals have survived past dangers and will continue to thrive in the future.
options.C: explaining how the black coral's damaged appearance hides its ability to survive.
options.D: sharing details about the qualities that make the black coral an unusual animal.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The author mentions Mesopotamia and kingdoms (paragraphs 1, 3, and 5) only briefly, to show how long the coral lives.
B. Incorrect. The idea that the corals “may outlast us” appears only at the end of paragraph 7; it is one detail, not the main way the author shares a point of view.
C. Incorrect. The contrast between the coral's battered look and its survival is the focus of paragraph 6 only.
D. CORRECT. Throughout the passage the author piles up details that show how unusual the black coral is: it grows on the remains of its ancestors (paragraph 2), grows “almost unbelievably slowly” (paragraph 3), survives as one organism for thousands of years (paragraph 4), and records the ocean's history in its rings (paragraph 5).

paragraphs.text: In the 1940s, pilots spoke of an invisible wall in the sky. As an airplane approached the speed of sound—about 760 miles per hour at sea level, and less in the thin, cold air high above—it began to buck and shudder, and some designers feared that any craft that tried to go faster would shake itself to pieces. Newspapers called it the “sound barrier,” and many people believed it was unbreakable. Even so, a small team of engineers and test pilots set out to fly through it. One of them was a twenty-four-year-old pilot from West Virginia named Chuck Yeager.

The barrier had already claimed a life. In September 1946, British pilot Geoffrey de Havilland Jr. was testing an experimental jet over the mouth of the Thames River when the plane broke apart as it neared the speed of sound. The crash was a terrible blow to the effort, and some engineers wondered whether the goal was worth the risk. Mindful of the tragedy, the American team working on a rocket plane called the X-1 decided that they would not try for the record in a single daring leap.

The team approached the challenge with patience and careful planning. Yeager would fly the X-1 a little faster on each flight, increasing its speed by only a few hundredths of the speed of sound at a time. After every flight, engineers studied the instruments and the pilot's report before allowing the next small step. The pilot, the plane, and the plan would be tested together, inch by inch.

By early October 1947, Yeager had pushed the X-1 to about 94 percent of the speed of sound, but at that speed a new problem appeared. Shock waves forming on the tail made the controls that tipped the plane's nose up and down stop working; the plane simply would not respond. Stuck at this point, the team needed a new idea. Engineer Jack Ridley suggested that Yeager steer with a part of the tail that was normally used only for small adjustments, moving the entire horizontal stabilizer instead. On the next flight, the trick worked, and Yeager felt ready to try for the record.

The attempt was scheduled for October 14, 1947, at Muroc Army Air Field in the California desert. Two nights earlier, Yeager went horseback riding in the dark, was thrown from his horse, and broke two ribs. Afraid that he would be pulled from the flight, he told almost no one. In pain, he could not push the X-1's door closed with his right arm, so Ridley cut off a piece of a broom handle that Yeager could use as a lever.

The X-1 did not take off from the ground like an ordinary plane. Its rocket engine burned fuel so quickly that it carried only about two and a half minutes of powered flight. To save every second, the X-1 was carried up in the belly of a large B-29 bomber and released at more than 20,000 feet. A second plane, called a chase plane, flew nearby to watch the X-1 and to help if anything went wrong.

That morning, the X-1 dropped from the bomber like a stone. Yeager fired its rockets one by one, and the plane shot upward, climbing past 40,000 feet. As he neared the speed of sound, the plane began to shake. For a moment, the needle on the Mach meter wavered. Then it jumped off the scale—and, to Yeager's astonishment, the violent shaking stopped and the ride turned smooth. On the ground, observers heard a deep boom roll across the desert. Yeager had reached about 700 miles per hour, or 1.06 times the speed of sound.

Within a few years, other pilots and planes were flying faster than sound, and a new age of flight had begun. From 1976 to 2003, the Concorde carried passengers across the Atlantic Ocean at twice the speed of sound. Since it was retired, no airline has offered supersonic travel, and some wonder whether ordinary passengers will ever fly that fast again. But perhaps there is another Yeager, a pilot or engineer who, with courage and patience, will make the impossible ordinary once again.

questions.question: The words “invisible wall,” “shake itself to pieces,” and “unbreakable” in paragraph 1 affect the tone of the paragraph because they

options.A: show how carefully engineers had studied the problem of flying at high speeds.
options.B: convey the rivalry among nations to build the fastest airplanes.
options.C: highlight the idea that only the most experienced pilots could fly at high speeds.
options.D: emphasize the idea that flying faster than sound seemed both impossible and deadly.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. These words describe how frightening and impossible the goal seemed, not how carefully engineers had studied it.
B. Incorrect. Paragraph 1 does not mention any competition between nations.
C. Incorrect. The words suggest that no airplane could survive going faster than sound, no matter how experienced the pilot was.
D. CORRECT. An “invisible wall” that is “unbreakable” suggests the goal could not be reached, and a plane that might “shake itself to pieces” suggests that trying was deadly. Together the words create a tone of fear and impossibility.

questions.question:
Read these sentences from paragraph 7.

“For a moment, the needle on the Mach meter wavered. Then it jumped off the scale—and, to Yeager's astonishment, the violent shaking stopped and the ride turned smooth.”

The sentences contribute to the development of ideas in the passage by showing that

options.A: the X-1 had been built to withstand far more shaking than other planes.
options.B: Yeager had finally stopped worrying about his injured ribs.
options.C: the sound barrier was not the deadly wall that many people had feared.
options.D: Yeager was proud that the team's step-by-step plan had worked perfectly.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The sentences say the shaking stopped once the plane passed the speed of sound; they do not compare the X-1's strength with that of other planes.
B. Incorrect. Yeager's ribs are not mentioned in these sentences; they focus on what happened to the plane.
C. CORRECT. Paragraph 1 describes the fear that a plane would “shake itself to pieces” at the speed of sound. Yeager's “astonishment” when “the violent shaking stopped and the ride turned smooth” shows that the barrier was far less dangerous to cross than people had believed.
D. Incorrect. The sentences describe Yeager's surprise at the smooth ride, not pride in the team's plan.

questions.question: Which sentence best supports the idea that the team needed an alternative to its “careful planning” (paragraph 3) in order to reach its goal?

options.A: “The crash was a terrible blow to the effort, and some engineers wondered whether the goal was worth the risk.” (paragraph 2)
options.B: “After every flight, engineers studied the instruments and the pilot's report before allowing the next small step.” (paragraph 3)
options.C: “Engineer Jack Ridley suggested that Yeager steer with a part of the tail that was normally used only for small adjustments, moving the entire horizontal stabilizer instead.” (paragraph 4)
options.D: “To save every second, the X-1 was carried up in the belly of a large B-29 bomber and released at more than 20,000 feet.” (paragraph 6)

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. This sentence describes doubts caused by the 1946 crash, which happened before the team's plan began.
B. Incorrect. This sentence describes the careful plan itself, not an alternative to it.
C. CORRECT. Paragraph 4 explains that the plan stalled at 94 percent of the speed of sound because the usual controls “stop[ped] working.” Ridley's idea of steering with a different part of the tail was a new solution that went beyond the step-by-step plan, and it allowed Yeager to continue.
D. Incorrect. Carrying the X-1 aloft was part of the normal method for every flight, not a new solution to a problem.

questions.question: Which sentence from the passage indicates that Yeager nearly made a mistake that could have cost him the chance to make the flight?

options.A: “By early October 1947, Yeager had pushed the X-1 to about 94 percent of the speed of sound, but at that speed a new problem appeared.” (paragraph 4)
options.B: “Two nights earlier, Yeager went horseback riding in the dark, was thrown from his horse, and broke two ribs.” (paragraph 5)
options.C: “A second plane, called a chase plane, flew nearby to watch the X-1 and to help if anything went wrong.” (paragraph 6)
options.D: “Yeager fired its rockets one by one, and the plane shot upward, climbing past 40,000 feet.” (paragraph 7)

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. This sentence describes a problem with the plane's controls, not a mistake that Yeager made.
B. CORRECT. Riding a horse in the dark just before the flight led to two broken ribs. Paragraph 5 explains that Yeager was “afraid that he would be pulled from the flight” and could not close the door without help, so this choice nearly cost him the record attempt.
C. Incorrect. The chase plane was a planned safety measure, not a mistake.
D. Incorrect. This sentence describes the flight going as planned.

questions.question: The 1946 crash described in paragraph 2 influenced the X-1 team's approach to the sound barrier by

options.A: convincing them to build a plane that was stronger than de Havilland's jet.
options.B: leading them to choose a more experienced pilot for the attempt.
options.C: persuading them to try for the record in a different country.
options.D: causing them to approach the speed of sound in small, careful steps.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The passage does not say the crash led the team to build a stronger plane.
B. Incorrect. The passage does not discuss how Yeager was chosen or compare his experience with that of other pilots.
C. Incorrect. The crash happened in Britain and the X-1 flights took place in California, but the passage never says the team chose the location because of the crash.
D. CORRECT. Paragraph 2 says that, “mindful of the tragedy,” the team decided not to try for the record “in a single daring leap.” Paragraph 3 then describes their plan to go “a little faster on each flight” and to test everything “inch by inch.”

paragraphs.text: It was then the custom of the directors of the Botanical Garden neither to hire plant hunters nor to send anyone abroad in search of rare specimens. The Garden depended instead upon gifts from the public, and I spent a good part of every day answering letters from people who wished to sell or donate plants. Some offered seeds from their grandmothers' gardens; others described “remarkable” shrubs that turned out to be common weeds. It was my duty to read each letter, to judge whether the plant described was worth having, and to write a polite reply.

To the owners of . . . wilted ferns, root-bound geraniums, and cactuses said to bloom once a century, I sent courteous but firm refusals—of course, first submitting every such letter, together with my answer, to Dr. Vell.

One afternoon late in April, however, just as I was putting on my coat to go home, the head gardener, Mr. Pruitt, called across the greenhouse that Dr. Vell wished to see me for a moment; so I hung up my coat again and climbed the narrow iron stairs to the little office above the palm house. Dr. Vell, who was sitting at his desk behind a stack of letters and replies that I had brought him for approval, lowered his spectacles and looked over them at me with a crooked smile that suggested amusement, impatience, mild irritation, and something very like an apology.
“Now, here is a letter,” he said, tapping a sheet of paper that lay apart from the others—“a letter that I suppose you remember.” He held it out to me.
“Oh yes,” I replied, with a shrug; “the man is clearly mistaken—or—”
“Or what?” asked Dr. Vell calmly, polishing his spectacles.
“—Or he is making it up,” I said.

After a pause he leaned back and asked me to read the letter to him again, and I did so in the tone one uses for a joke that has gone on too long. The writer, I said, must be either a very simple man or a very clever trickster. To my surprise, Dr. Vell did not laugh.
“I suppose,” he said, with his shy, near-sighted smile, “that nine people out of ten would toss that letter into the wastebasket and call the writer a fool or a fraud?”
“In my opinion,” I said, “he is one or the other.”
“He isn't—in mine,” said Dr. Vell quietly.
“But sir!” I exclaimed. “Here is a lighthouse keeper living alone on a rock at the edge of the sea, who wants us to send someone to collect a flower that no longer exists!”
“And how do you know,” asked Dr. Vell, “that the flower does not exist?”

“It is generally agreed,” I answered, rather sharply, “that the Corran ghost orchid has been extinct for fifty years. So you may forgive me for doubting that our lighthouse keeper has three of them growing in a tin washtub.”
“Ah, you young scientists,” said Dr. Vell, smiling tiredly, “you build your conclusions the way children build castles in the sand.”
He leaned back in his chair, his eyes wandering toward the window as though he could see the picture he was describing.
“Very fine and very certain—until the tide comes in. And it always comes in, doesn't it?”
My face growing warm, I said, “Then you don't believe the ghost orchid is extinct?”
“Thomas Pell drew one from life in 1871.”
“And who has seen a living one since?”
“No one—except our lighthouse keeper,” he answered, laughing.
I laughed too, thinking the matter was settled, but Dr. Vell went on, quite seriously:
“Whatever it is that Mr. Crane has found—and I am daring to hope it is the ghost orchid itself—I want you to bring it here for the Garden.”
When my surprise had passed, the first thing I felt was pity. Plainly, poor Dr. Vell's judgment was failing him at last—what a loss to science!

I believe now that Dr. Vell understood exactly what I was thinking, but he showed neither offense nor impatience. I pulled a chair up beside his desk—there was nothing to do but follow orders, and this wild-goose chase was certainly not my idea.
Together we listed the supplies I would need and the costs I might expect, and I set a date for my return that left no time at all for actually finding anything.
“Never mind the date,” said Dr. Vell. “What I want is for you to bring those orchids back alive. Now, how many crates will you need?”
“One,” I replied flatly; “anything more is a waste of money, unless there is something to carry home. If there is, I'll telegraph you at once.”
“Very well,” said Dr. Vell cheerfully, “you shall have whatever help you ask for. Can you leave on the morning train?”
He certainly did not waste time. I nodded, a little sulkily, knowing that he was amused.

“So,” I said, picking up my hat, “I am to travel to a place called Gull Point, where a man named Crane keeps, along with his lamp oil and his fishing nets, a flower that vanished from the earth half a century ago—”
By now we were both laughing. I asked him why in the world he trusted the word of a man he had never met.

“I suppose,” he answered, with the same half-sheepish, half-amused smile, “it is a feeling. I simply feel that this Mr. Crane has found something real. I can't shake the idea that we are about to recover a flower the whole world has given up for lost. There—you think I am a foolish old man, don't you?”
But I did not think so; in fact, I noticed that the same strange hope that Dr. Vell felt was beginning, against my will, to quicken my own heartbeat.
“If he really has—” I began, then stopped.
Dr. Vell and I looked at each other for a long moment without speaking.
“Go on,” he said gently.
But I had nothing more to say, for the thought of seeing with my own eyes a living ghost orchid stirred up so many feelings at once that words seemed useless.

questions.question:
Read paragraph 2 from the story.

“To the owners of . . . wilted ferns, root-bound geraniums, and cactuses said to bloom once a century, I sent courteous but firm refusals—of course, first submitting every such letter, together with my answer, to Dr. Vell.”

This paragraph helps develop the plot by establishing that the narrator

options.A: believes that many of the plants offered are not worth adding to the Garden.
options.B: dislikes having to write refusal letters to members of the public.
options.C: tries to guess how Dr. Vell will respond to each letter.
options.D: resents Dr. Vell's habit of reviewing every reply.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. CORRECT. The “firm refusals” and the unflattering descriptions of the plants (“wilted ferns, root-bound geraniums”) show that the narrator judges most offers to be worthless, which sets up the narrator's quick dismissal of the lighthouse keeper's letter.
B. Incorrect. The refusals are “courteous,” and nothing in the paragraph suggests the narrator dislikes the work.
C. Incorrect. The narrator is confident in each answer; there is no sign of trying to guess what Dr. Vell will say.
D. Incorrect. The phrase “of course” shows that submitting the letters is a normal routine, not something the narrator resents.

questions.question:
Read this sentence from paragraph 3.

“Dr. Vell, who was sitting at his desk behind a stack of letters and replies that I had brought him for approval, lowered his spectacles and looked over them at me with a crooked smile that suggested amusement, impatience, mild irritation, and something very like an apology.”

What does the phrase “something very like an apology” convey about Dr. Vell?

options.A: It suggests that he is sorry for keeping the narrator late after work.
options.B: It shows that he is nervous about sharing his opinions with the narrator.
options.C: It suggests that he knows the conversation ahead will frustrate the narrator.
options.D: It implies that he is uncomfortable criticizing the narrator's replies.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. Dr. Vell is not apologizing for the hour; later he asks the narrator to leave “on the morning train,” which shows he is not worried about the narrator's time.
B. Incorrect. Dr. Vell states his opinions calmly and directly throughout the conversation (“He isn't—in mine”).
C. CORRECT. Dr. Vell is about to send the narrator on a trip the narrator considers foolish. His slightly apologetic look shows he expects the narrator to be annoyed, which is exactly what happens.
D. Incorrect. The conversation is about one letter and the trip, not about criticizing the narrator's replies.

questions.question: How does the exchange between Dr. Vell and the narrator in paragraphs 8–11 contribute to the development of the characters?

options.A: It reveals that the narrator is more careful than Dr. Vell, who believes whatever he reads.
options.B: It suggests that the narrator and Dr. Vell usually agree about which plants to accept.
options.C: It hints that the narrator will soon accept Dr. Vell's opinion about the letter.
options.D: It establishes a conflict between the narrator and Dr. Vell over whether the letter can be trusted.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. Dr. Vell does not believe everything he reads; he approves the narrator's other refusals and simply thinks this one letter deserves a closer look.
B. Incorrect. These paragraphs show the two characters disagreeing, not agreeing.
C. Incorrect. In these paragraphs the narrator is firm (“he is one or the other”); the narrator's change of heart comes much later, in paragraph 34.
D. CORRECT. The narrator calls the writer “a fool or a fraud,” while Dr. Vell answers, “He isn't—in mine.” This exchange sets up the central disagreement of the story.

questions.question: Dr. Vell's observations in paragraphs 15–17 create tension in the story by causing the narrator to feel

options.A: frustrated by Dr. Vell's lack of interest in the narrator's work.
options.B: embarrassed by Dr. Vell's criticism of how the narrator reasons.
options.C: confused by Dr. Vell's comparison of scientists to children.
options.D: annoyed by Dr. Vell's teasing about the lighthouse keeper.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. Dr. Vell's comments are about how young scientists reach conclusions, not about whether the narrator's work is interesting.
B. CORRECT. Dr. Vell says young scientists build conclusions like “castles in the sand” that are “very certain—until the tide comes in,” which criticizes the narrator's certainty. The narrator's reaction, “My face growing warm,” shows embarrassment.
C. Incorrect. The narrator understands the comparison well enough to be stung by it and replies right away.
D. Incorrect. Dr. Vell's observations in these paragraphs are about the narrator's way of thinking, not about the lighthouse keeper.

questions.question: How does the interaction between the narrator and Dr. Vell in paragraphs 26–28 contribute to the development of the theme?

options.A: It shows the narrator's acceptance of the assignment despite personal doubts about it.
options.B: It illustrates Dr. Vell's patience as the narrator argues against making the trip.
options.C: It reveals the narrator's frustration at having little say in the Garden's decisions.
options.D: It emphasizes Dr. Vell's willingness to spend any amount of money on rare plants.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. CORRECT. The narrator helps plan the trip but sets a return date that leaves “no time at all for actually finding anything” and asks for only one crate, calling more “a waste of money.” The narrator goes along with the assignment while still doubting it.
B. Incorrect. The narrator does not argue against the trip itself, only against taking more crates than necessary.
C. Incorrect. Although the narrator did not choose the trip, these paragraphs focus on planning it, not on complaints about the Garden's decisions.
D. Incorrect. Dr. Vell offers “whatever help you ask for,” but the paragraphs do not suggest he would spend any amount of money.

questions.question: Which sentence from the story best explains why Dr. Vell is eager to send the narrator to Gull Point?

options.A: “Plainly, poor Dr. Vell's judgment was failing him at last—what a loss to science!” (paragraph 24)
options.B: “‘What I want is for you to bring those orchids back alive.’” (paragraph 27)
options.C: “‘I can't shake the idea that we are about to recover a flower the whole world has given up for lost.’” (paragraph 33)
options.D: “But I did not think so; in fact, I noticed that the same strange hope that Dr. Vell felt was beginning, against my will, to quicken my own heartbeat.” (paragraph 34)

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. This sentence shows what the narrator thinks of Dr. Vell, not Dr. Vell's reason for wanting the trip.
B. Incorrect. This sentence shows what Dr. Vell wants the narrator to do, but not why he is so eager.
C. CORRECT. Dr. Vell explains his eagerness directly: he believes they may be about to recover a flower that “the whole world has given up for lost.”
D. Incorrect. This sentence describes the narrator's growing hope, not Dr. Vell's reason.

questions.question: How does paragraph 34 help develop the plot of the story?

options.A: It shows that the narrator feels pressure to finish the trip quickly.
options.B: It establishes that the narrator is willing to let Dr. Vell overrule the narrator's opinion.
options.C: It shows the narrator struggling to understand why Dr. Vell believes the letter.
options.D: It shows that the narrator is beginning to believe the orchid might really be found.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. Paragraph 34 is about the narrator's feelings of hope, not about time pressure.
B. Incorrect. The narrator already agreed to follow orders in paragraph 25; paragraph 34 shows a change in what the narrator believes, not a willingness to be overruled.
C. Incorrect. By paragraph 34, the narrator is not puzzling over Dr. Vell's reasons but sharing his feeling.
D. CORRECT. After doubting the letter throughout the story, the narrator admits that “the same strange hope that Dr. Vell felt” is beginning “to quicken my own heartbeat,” a turning point that sets up the journey to come.

questions.question: Which sentence best demonstrates the professional relationship between the narrator and Dr. Vell?

options.B: “Plainly, poor Dr. Vell's judgment was failing him at last—what a loss to science!” (paragraph 24)
options.C: “I pulled a chair up beside his desk—there was nothing to do but follow orders, and this wild-goose chase was certainly not my idea.” (paragraph 25)
options.D: “‘Very well,’ said Dr. Vell cheerfully, ‘you shall have whatever help you ask for.’” (paragraph 29)

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. Handing over a letter does not show who is in charge of whom.
B. Incorrect. This is the narrator's private reaction to Dr. Vell's idea, not a description of their working relationship.
C. CORRECT. The narrator thinks the trip is a “wild-goose chase” but has “nothing to do but follow orders,” which shows that Dr. Vell is the narrator's boss and the narrator must do as he says.
D. Incorrect. Dr. Vell's offer of help shows his generosity but does not clearly show their roles.

questions.question: How does the author develop the contrast between the narrator's point of view and Dr. Vell's point of view?

options.A: by using the conversation between the two characters to show their different reactions to the letter
options.B: by describing Dr. Vell's repeated attempts to change the narrator's mind about the letter
options.C: by including dialogue that explains why Dr. Vell is in charge of the narrator
options.D: by sharing both characters' thoughts about how age affects a person's judgment

solution.exhibit_text:
A. CORRECT. Nearly the whole story is a conversation in which the narrator mocks the letter (“he is making it up”) while Dr. Vell takes it seriously (“He isn't—in mine”), so their dialogue is the main way the contrast is developed.
B. Incorrect. Dr. Vell does not keep trying to persuade the narrator; he simply gives the assignment.
C. Incorrect. The story shows that Dr. Vell is in charge but never explains why.
D. Incorrect. Dr. Vell comments on “young scientists” once, but the characters do not share their thoughts about age and judgment in any detail.

ela_passages.title: Looking for the Universe's First Morning
ela_passages.intro_text: Launched in 2021, the James Webb Space Telescope orbits about one million miles from Earth. Its gold-coated mirror, more than 21 feet across, collects faint infrared light from some of the first galaxies that formed in the universe.

lines.text: There are the things that are close to us,
things we can reach and hold, and then
there are the things so far away that their light
is older than the oceans, older than the Earth.
So beyond the Moon are the planets,
and beyond the planets are the stars,
and beyond the stars, the galaxies; and beyond those—
what, exactly? Because we are talking about
the beginning here: the start of your shoelace,
the cereal going soggy in your bowl,
the bus that hissed and groaned this morning,
your grandmother, and the silver ring
she turns and turns around her finger
when she is thinking. And the beginning of thinking.
Everything and everywhere
began in the same place, wherever
it was. How do we find it? We can read it
in the oldest rocks, in their slow
handwriting of layers. Or we can fold
a mirror small enough to fit inside a rocket
and send it a million miles from home,
where it opens in the cold and the dark
(like a flower at sunrise, only a flower
made of gold, unfolding petal by petal)
and turns its back on the Sun, and waits,
and waits, until the faintest glow of the first light
drips into its golden cup like honey.
And there, in the blackness, in the silence,
barely brighter than nothing, they appear:
the protogalaxies, the quasars, the nebulae,
the red dwarfs and the white dwarfs. Their names
sound like villains in a comic book, or maybe
spells a wizard mutters when he's lost his keys.
The one thing we know for sure
is that their light is old. This is how the past
enters our world, how the iron in your blood
and the ice in the rings of Saturn
were cooked inside the same first stars,
scattered apart, and carried here. It is only out there,
in the cold—in the vast dark attic
where astronomers sort
through what they can, whatever arrives intact—
that the universe lets us see its baby pictures,
glowing with the light of its first morning.

questions.question: Read lines 5–8 from the poem. The lines help develop a central idea of the poem by revealing the speaker's

options.A: curiosity about what lies beyond everything that can be seen.
options.B: interest in measuring the distances between the planets and the stars.
options.C: desire to prove that there are galaxies beyond our own.
options.D: questions about which tools are needed to study distant galaxies.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. CORRECT. Lines 5–8 move outward step by step (“beyond the Moon … beyond the planets … beyond the stars”) and end with the question “what, exactly?”, which shows the speaker's curiosity about what lies past everything we know.
B. Incorrect. The lines list what lies beyond what, but they say nothing about measuring distances.
C. Incorrect. The speaker already names “the galaxies” as known; the question is about what lies beyond them, not about proving they exist.
D. Incorrect. Tools such as the mirror are introduced later, in the second stanza; lines 5–8 do not ask about tools.

questions.question: The main purpose of the comparison in lines 23–24 of the poem is to show

options.A: how large the telescope's mirror is.
options.B: how the mirror opens up once it is in space.
options.C: that the mirror has a familiar color.
options.D: how the mirror can work only in the cold.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The comparison describes the mirror's movement, not its size.
B. CORRECT. Comparing the mirror to “a flower at sunrise … unfolding petal by petal” shows how the folded mirror opens up piece by piece after it reaches space (“where it opens in the cold and the dark,” line 22).
C. Incorrect. The mirror is “made of gold,” but the point of the comparison is the unfolding, not the color.
D. Incorrect. The cold is mentioned in line 22, but the comparison itself is about how the mirror opens.

questions.question: Read lines 26–27 from the poem. The imagery in the lines reveals that the speaker

options.A: envies the astronomers who study the oldest light.
options.B: has personally seen the first galaxies through a telescope.
options.C: has a simple understanding of how telescopes work.
options.D: marvels at the way the telescope gathers such faint, distant light.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The astronomers are not mentioned until line 41; lines 26–27 focus on the telescope and the light.
B. Incorrect. The speaker describes what the telescope does, not something the speaker has personally seen.
C. Incorrect. The image of light that “drips into its golden cup like honey” is a poetic description, not a sign of a simple understanding.
D. CORRECT. The repetition “and waits, / and waits” and the image of “the faintest glow of the first light” dripping in “like honey” show the speaker's wonder at how slowly and gently the telescope collects light from so far away.

questions.question: Read lines 31–33 from the poem. The speaker refers to familiar things in the lines most likely to

options.A: explain confusing scientific information in simple terms.
options.B: suggest that the scientific names for objects in space sound silly by making a humorous comparison.
options.C: emphasize that the study of distant galaxies is still in its early stages.
options.D: demonstrate how ideas about space can be explained with situations from everyday life.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The speaker does not explain what quasars or nebulae are; the lines only comment on how their names sound.
B. CORRECT. Saying the names “sound like villains in a comic book” or “spells a wizard mutters when he's lost his keys” is a playful way of suggesting that the scientific vocabulary sounds odd and a little silly.
C. Incorrect. Nothing in the lines suggests that the research is new or unfinished.
D. Incorrect. The comic book and the wizard describe the sound of the names, not any scientific idea.

questions.question: Read lines 35–38 from the poem. The poet includes these lines most likely to emphasize that

options.A: astronomers must keep studying the first stars to understand Saturn.
options.B: the light from the first stars is too faint to tell us very much.
options.C: the first stars made the materials found in everything, near and far.
options.D: the study of the human body and the study of planets are alike.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The lines explain where materials came from; they do not argue that more research about Saturn is needed.
B. Incorrect. The lines describe how important the first stars are, not how little their light can tell us.
C. CORRECT. “The iron in your blood” and “the ice in the rings of Saturn” are very different and very far apart, yet both “were cooked inside the same first stars.” This connects back to the idea that “Everything and everywhere / began in the same place” (lines 15–16).
D. Incorrect. The lines connect blood and Saturn through where their materials came from, not by comparing two areas of study.

questions.question: Read lines 39–44 from the poem. The lines reveal the speaker's

options.A: frustration with the tools that astronomers must use.
options.B: belief that astronomers are racing to make a discovery before others do.
options.C: interest in astronomers and their study of the early universe.
options.D: certainty that astronomers keep their findings secret.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The images in these lines (“baby pictures,” “the light of its first morning”) are warm and positive, not frustrated.
B. Incorrect. The astronomers “sort / through what they can” patiently; nothing suggests they are racing anyone.
C. CORRECT. The speaker describes astronomers sorting through “whatever arrives intact” in “the vast dark attic” of space and treats their work as a rare chance to see the universe's “baby pictures,” which shows interest and admiration.
D. Incorrect. Although the “dark attic” may suggest hidden things, it refers to the hidden early universe, not to secret work by astronomers.

ela_passages.title: Hungry Helpers on the Hillside

paragraphs.text: Inside a regional park in the dry hills of Northern California, a herd of about four hundred goats moves slowly across a steep slope, munching as it goes. The hills are home to hundreds of kinds of plants and animals, from tiny wildflowers to black-tailed deer. While goats are known for eating almost anything—including plants that people would rather keep—a carefully managed herd is actually one of the best tools for protecting this landscape.

Wildfires are a natural part of life in these hills, and when dry brush builds up, the results can be disastrous. However, hundreds of years ago, herders in the hills of Spain and other lands around the Mediterranean Sea noticed something useful. When fire swept across the countryside, it often slowed down or even stopped where goats had been grazing, because the animals had eaten much of the brush that would have fed the flames. Herders began to graze their goats deliberately on the slopes around their villages, creating strips of bare land that helped keep fires away from their homes.

Today land managers in the park and ranchers across the western United States continue to use goats to care for the land. Grazing can dramatically improve the health of the plants that grow back. Goats strip away thick, weedy brush and trim back young shrubs and trees, leaving more water, sunlight, and nutrients for the plants that remain. In addition, as the goats move across the land, their droppings return nutrients to the soil, and their hooves press seeds into the ground.

One common target of grazing in the park is an invasive shrub called French broom. A single broom plant can produce thousands of seeds each year, and those seeds can survive in the soil for decades. The shrubs grow so thick and tall that they block sunlight from reaching the plants beneath them. The fast-spreading broom tends to crowd out native grasses and wildflowers, the main source of food for many of the insects, birds, and deer that live in the hills. When broom dries out in summer, it also becomes fuel for fire. An imbalance in one part of the hills' ecosystem affects the entire web of life. Grazing helps restore this delicate balance.

Of course, the goats are meant to graze only part of the land at a time. A herd left to wander freely would eat everything in its path, including young native plants and the shrubs that shelter nesting birds. The key to using goats is knowing where to graze and for how long. Land managers in the park use a method called rotational grazing, meaning they move the herd from one section of land to another. They study the land to find out which areas most need grazing, and then they surround one section at a time with a portable electric fence. The goats stay in that section for only a few days before they are moved. While the herd works on the next section, the land behind it has time to rest and regrow, often healthier than before.

Researchers have counted the plants and animals in the grazed areas, and their studies show that rotational grazing has helped native wildflowers and grasses return to slopes where broom had crowded them out. The program has worked so well that the park's staff now teach ranchers and neighborhood groups how to plan grazing projects of their own. Turning a herd of hungry goats loose on a hillside may seem reckless, but carefully planned grazing has protected hillsides for centuries and, with careful management, will continue to do so.
