questions.question: According to the passage, how did wildfires prompt herders to begin grazing goats on purpose?

options.A: by driving the goats to safer pastures closer to the villages
options.B: by destroying the crops that herders had planted to feed their animals
options.C: by revealing that fires slowed down where goats had eaten away the brush
options.D: by clearing the land so that tender new grass grew for the goats to eat

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The passage does not say that fires drove goats closer to the villages.
B. Incorrect. The passage does not mention fires destroying crops planted for animals.
C. CORRECT. Paragraph 2 says that fire “often slowed down or even stopped where goats had been grazing, because the animals had eaten much of the brush that would have fed the flames.” This observation led herders to graze goats “deliberately” around their villages.
D. Incorrect. The passage does not say that fire created new grass for goats; the herders' discovery was about how goats affected fire, not how fire affected goats.

questions.question: Targeting French broom with grazing affects the animals that live in the hills mostly by

options.A: reducing the shelter that birds use for building their nests.
options.B: endangering the animals that live in the broom shrubs.
options.C: making sure that the animals have enough water to drink.
options.D: ensuring that the grasses and wildflowers the animals depend on for food can thrive.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. Paragraph 5 mentions shrubs that shelter birds, but only as something a free-roaming herd might harm, not as the main effect of targeting broom.
B. Incorrect. The passage does not say that animals live in the broom or are endangered by grazing it.
C. Incorrect. Paragraph 3 says grazing leaves more water for plants, but paragraph 4 does not connect broom to the animals' drinking water.
D. CORRECT. Paragraph 4 explains that broom “tends to crowd out native grasses and wildflowers, the main source of food for many of the insects, birds, and deer that live in the hills.” Removing the broom lets those food plants grow.

questions.question:
Read this sentence from paragraph 6.

“The program has worked so well that the park's staff now teach ranchers and neighborhood groups how to plan grazing projects of their own.”

The author includes this sentence to show that

options.A: the park's staff are better qualified to manage land than ranchers are.
options.B: the park's staff are eager to involve others in caring for the land.
options.C: the grazing program will return the hills to their original condition.
options.D: the park's teaching program should be copied by every park in the country.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. Teaching ranchers suggests the staff believe ranchers can run their own projects, not that the staff are better qualified.
B. CORRECT. Because the program “has worked so well,” the staff share what they have learned so that ranchers and neighbors can protect their own land too.
C. Incorrect. The sentence is about teaching others, not about returning the hills to an original condition.
D. Incorrect. The sentence does not say other parks should copy the program.

questions.question: Which sentence supports the idea that people who manage land may be concerned about using goats as a way to benefit the land?

options.A: “While goats are known for eating almost anything—including plants that people would rather keep—a carefully managed herd is actually one of the best tools for protecting this landscape.” (paragraph 1)
options.B: “Herders began to graze their goats deliberately on the slopes around their villages, creating strips of bare land that helped keep fires away from their homes.” (paragraph 2)
options.C: “In addition, as the goats move across the land, their droppings return nutrients to the soil, and their hooves press seeds into the ground.” (paragraph 3)
options.D: “The goats stay in that section for only a few days before they are moved.” (paragraph 5)

solution.exhibit_text:
A. CORRECT. This sentence admits that goats eat “almost anything—including plants that people would rather keep,” which explains why land managers might worry about turning goats loose on their land.
B. Incorrect. This sentence describes how herders benefited from grazing, not why anyone might be concerned.
C. Incorrect. This sentence describes benefits of grazing.
D. Incorrect. This sentence describes how the rotation works, not a reason for concern.

questions.question:
Read this sentence from paragraph 6.

“Turning a herd of hungry goats loose on a hillside may seem reckless, but carefully planned grazing has protected hillsides for centuries and, with careful management, will continue to do so.”

The words “reckless” and “carefully planned” convey the idea that

options.A: the safest methods are sometimes the least effective at solving difficult problems.
options.B: trying unusual methods almost always leads to surprising results.
options.C: careful planning can make sure that a potentially destructive action has a positive result.
options.D: plans that involve some risk are usually more successful than plans that do not.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The passage presents grazing as both effective and well managed, not as an unsafe method that works better than safe ones.
B. Incorrect. Grazing is not presented as an unusual method; herders have used it “for centuries.”
C. CORRECT. “Reckless” admits that a hungry herd could do damage, while “carefully planned” shows that planning (choosing sections, fencing, moving the herd) turns that risky action into one that helps the land.
D. Incorrect. The sentence does not claim that risky plans are generally more successful.

questions.question: With which statement would the author most likely agree?

options.A: It is important to warn people who live nearby before goats are brought into a park.
options.B: It is necessary to study an area carefully in order to plan a successful grazing project.
options.C: Counting plants after grazing is a minor part of the researchers' work.
options.D: Land managers should consider the benefits of French broom before removing it.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The passage does not discuss warning neighbors.
B. CORRECT. Paragraph 5 says “the key to using goats is knowing where to graze and for how long” and that land managers “study the land to find out which areas most need grazing” before fencing a section.
C. Incorrect. Paragraph 6 presents the researchers' counts as the evidence that the program works, so the author treats them as important.
D. Incorrect. The author describes broom only as harmful: it shades out other plants, crowds out food sources, and fuels fires.

questions.question: How do the diagram and its text provide additional support for the topic presented in the passage?

options.A: by showing that rotational grazing works best on the steepest slopes
options.B: by revealing that goats are used mainly on land where no people live
options.C: by depicting how the land in each section changes as the herd is rotated
options.D: by comparing the number of goats needed for large and small sections of land

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The diagram does not show or compare slopes.
B. Incorrect. The diagram does not say anything about where people live.
C. CORRECT. The diagram shows three sections side by side: thick broom that has not been grazed yet, a section the goats are clearing this week, and a section grazed last year where “native grasses and wildflowers grow back.” Together they show how the land changes as the herd moves, supporting paragraph 5's description of rotational grazing.
D. Incorrect. The diagram does not give or compare numbers of goats.

lines.text: I know already what this place becomes.
The shops will paper over their windows,
the carousel will wear a canvas hood,
and the boardwalk will belong to the gulls.
The wind will sharpen its teeth.
But not yet. Not yet.
Right now it is the last warm week of August,
the sea still holding the heat of July
while the evenings fold up a little earlier,
and a cool breath slips off the water
to rest on my shoulders like a hand
that knows me, there and then gone.
But once the ferry quits running in October,
that hand, I know, will become a shove,
the kind a stranger gives you
hurrying past on a crowded street.
So I am taking the long way home tonight,
past the rental shed with its stack of striped umbrellas,
past cottages painted mint and lemon and coral
like a tin of buttons my grandmother promised to give me
and then forgot. How strange to miss
a place while I am still standing in it.
These slow gold evenings leave me
alone with a quiet that fits me
better than any jacket, and I know
how seldom anything fits like that.

questions.question: How does the structure of the poem affect the poem's meaning?

options.A: The lack of a rhyming pattern suggests that each summer day is unlike any other.
options.B: The single long stanza reflects the continuous flow of the speaker's thoughts.
options.C: The varied lengths of the sentences show how complicated the speaker's ideas are.
options.D: The use of complete sentences shows the speaker's appreciation for the clear start and end of each season.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The poem does not rhyme, but the lack of rhyme is not connected to the idea that each day is different; the poem is about the change from one season to the next.
B. CORRECT. The poem has no stanza breaks; the speaker's thoughts move without pause from the coming winter (lines 1–6) to the present evening (lines 7–12), back to October (lines 13–16), and then to the walk home (lines 17–26), like one long stream of thought.
C. Incorrect. The poem has both long and short sentences (“But not yet. Not yet.”), but sentence length is not used to show how complicated the ideas are.
D. Incorrect. The speaker focuses on the blurry edge between summer and fall, not on clear starts and ends of seasons.

questions.question: Which lines support the idea that a change in the season will lessen the speaker's enjoyment of the town?

options.A: “Right now it is the last warm week of August, / the sea still holding the heat of July” (lines 7–8)
options.B: “and a cool breath slips off the water / to rest on my shoulders like a hand” (lines 10–11)
options.C: “But once the ferry quits running in October, / that hand, I know, will become a shove,” (lines 13–14)
options.D: “So I am taking the long way home tonight, / past the rental shed with its stack of striped umbrellas,” (lines 17–18)

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. These lines describe the pleasant present, when the sea is “still holding the heat of July.”
B. Incorrect. These lines describe a gentle, friendly breeze that the speaker enjoys now.
C. CORRECT. Once the ferry stops in October, the gentle “hand” of the breeze “will become a shove,” which shows that the colder season will turn something the speaker enjoys into something unwelcome.
D. Incorrect. These lines show the speaker choosing to enjoy the town tonight by “taking the long way home.”

questions.question:
Read lines 5–6 from the poem.

“The wind will sharpen its teeth. / But not yet. Not yet.”

How do the lines develop a central theme of the poem?

options.A: They show the order in which the changes in the town will happen.
options.B: They emphasize the importance of valuing the present.
options.C: They warn about a danger that requires careful preparation.
options.D: They highlight a contrast between summer visitors and winter visitors.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The lines mention one future change, the sharper wind, but they do not put a series of changes in order.
B. CORRECT. Line 5 admits that harsh weather is coming, but the repeated “But not yet. Not yet.” turns the speaker's attention back to the present, which the rest of the poem shows the speaker savoring.
C. Incorrect. The speaker does not prepare for the wind; the speaker chooses to enjoy the time before it arrives.
D. Incorrect. The lines do not mention visitors at all.

questions.question:
Read lines 7–9 from the poem.

“Right now it is the last warm week of August, / the sea still holding the heat of July / while the evenings fold up a little earlier,”

The word choice in the lines helps convey the speaker's belief that

options.A: the end of summer is the least pleasant part of the year.
options.B: the change from one season to the next happens suddenly and without warning.
options.C: the change in the season is so slight that few people notice it.
options.D: the warmth of the current season should still be appreciated.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. Phrases such as “last warm week” and “still holding the heat” describe the season fondly, not as unpleasant.
B. Incorrect. The evenings shorten only “a little earlier,” which suggests a gradual change, not a sudden one.
C. Incorrect. The speaker clearly notices the change and describes it closely, so it is not presented as something people miss.
D. CORRECT. “Right now,” “last warm week,” and “still holding the heat” stress that summer's warmth is still here, which shows the speaker believes in enjoying it while it lasts.

questions.question: Which idea does the comparison of the cottages to “a tin of buttons my grandmother promised to give me / and then forgot” in lines 20–21 convey?

options.A: It reveals that the speaker is still upset about a broken promise.
options.B: It suggests that the speaker has wanted to live in the town since childhood.
options.C: It indicates that the town the speaker is walking through is colorful and charming.
options.D: It suggests that people often hold on to regrets from the past.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The grandmother's promise is a small, gentle detail; the speaker does not express anger about it.
B. Incorrect. The comparison is about how the cottages look, not about the speaker's childhood plans.
C. CORRECT. Cottages “painted mint and lemon and coral” look like a tin of bright buttons, a treasure a child would love. The comparison shows how delightful and appealing the town looks to the speaker.
D. Incorrect. Although the promise was forgotten, the poem does not develop an idea about people holding on to regrets.

questions.question:
Read these lines from the poem.

“I know already what this place becomes.” (line 1)

“How strange to miss / a place while I am still standing in it.” (lines 21–22)

The lines develop a central idea of the poem by

options.A: emphasizing the speaker's awareness that the present moment will soon be something to miss.
options.B: suggesting the speaker's wish to escape the repetitive routine of life in the town.
options.C: revealing the speaker's disappointment that the seasons always change the same way.
options.D: showing that the speaker expects to feel certain emotions because the speaker knows the town so well.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. CORRECT. Line 1 shows the speaker knows the town will soon become empty and cold, and lines 21–22 show the speaker already missing the town “while I am still standing in it.” Together they show the speaker treasuring the present because it will soon be gone.
B. Incorrect. The speaker does not want to escape; the speaker is “taking the long way home” to enjoy the town.
C. Incorrect. The speaker accepts the change of seasons; the lines express fondness, not disappointment.
D. Incorrect. The speaker does know the town, but the lines focus on valuing the present moment, not on predicting particular feelings.

questions.question: The speaker's thoughts throughout the poem develop a theme by showing that

options.A: although people come from many different places, most are drawn to the charm of a seaside town.
options.B: although people can plan their lives, some things will always be beyond their control.
options.C: although people may expect changes ahead, some long to hold on to present experiences while they are still happening.
options.D: although people have general expectations, they cannot know what any single day will bring.

solution.exhibit_text:
A. Incorrect. The poem focuses on one speaker's feelings about one town, not on why people in general are drawn to the shore.
B. Incorrect. The speaker cannot stop the season from changing, but the poem focuses on enjoying the present rather than on what cannot be controlled.
C. CORRECT. The speaker knows exactly what is coming (“The wind will sharpen its teeth”) but chooses to savor the present (“But not yet. Not yet.”) and even misses the town while still in it.
D. Incorrect. The speaker is quite sure what will happen; the poem is not about the unpredictability of each day.

sentence_paragraphs.text: In 2004, a spacecraft named Cassini, built by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) together with space agencies in Europe and Italy, arrived at the planet Saturn.
The spacecraft’s mission was to study Saturn, its rings, and its many moons.
Cassini was designed to orbit Saturn for about four years, but its assignment did not come to an end until more than 13 years later in 2017.
During its mission, Cassini flew close to Enceladus, a small, icy moon of Saturn.
Its cameras revealed long cracks near the moon’s south pole.
Scientists nicknamed these cracks “tiger stripes” because of their resemblance to the markings on a tiger’s fur.
These cracks were important because jets of water vapor and ice shooting out of them suggested that a liquid ocean might lie beneath the moon’s frozen surface.
Cassini continued to provide valuable data about Saturn’s rings, storms, and other moons.
Throughout the mission, the spacecraft circled Saturn 294 times.
In 2005, it released a probe called Huygens, which parachuted onto Titan, Saturn’s largest moon, and became the first spacecraft to land on a world in the outer solar system.
However, by 2017, the spacecraft was running low on fuel, putting the mission’s future in doubt.
Prior to this fuel shortage, the team had regularly fired Cassini’s thrusters to steer it safely past Saturn’s moons.
These maneuvers used up much of the spacecraft’s fuel.
Scientists then had to decide how to end the mission safely.
They chose to send Cassini on a series of 22 daring dives through the gap between Saturn and its rings, a stage they called the Grand Finale.
On September 15, 2017, the spacecraft plunged into Saturn’s atmosphere, sending back data until the very end.
In this way, NASA made sure that Cassini would never crash into and contaminate a moon that might hold life.
Cassini was an important asset in scientists’ study of Saturn; it returned more than 450,000 images and made discoveries that no one had expected.
Scientists expect to keep studying the data it collected for decades.
Even though Cassini’s journey has ended, a new mission called Dragonfly is planned to fly to Titan in the 2030s.

questions.question: Which sentence should follow sentence 3 to **best** introduce the topic of the passage?

options.A: The Cassini mission was a success because it proved that Saturn’s moon Enceladus is home to living things.
options.B: Throughout the Cassini mission, NASA scientists had to solve problems caused by flaws in the spacecraft’s design.
options.C: The Cassini mission lasted far longer than planned and allowed scientists to take additional photographs of Saturn.
options.D: Despite the challenges of exploring a distant planet, the Cassini spacecraft made many valuable discoveries about Saturn and its moons.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the sentence that should follow sentence 3 to best introduce the topic of the passage.

A. Incorrect. The passage says the jets on Enceladus “suggested” an ocean might exist; it never says Cassini proved that living things are there.
B. Incorrect. The passage does not describe any flaws in the spacecraft’s design. Its main challenge was running low on fuel.
C. Incorrect. The passage does say the mission lasted longer than planned, but photographs are only one small detail. This sentence leaves out the discoveries that the rest of the passage describes.
D. CORRECT. The passage describes Cassini’s discoveries (the “tiger stripes” and a possible ocean on Enceladus, the Huygens landing on Titan, more than 450,000 images) and its challenges (the fuel shortage and how to end the mission safely). This sentence previews both.

questions.question: Which word should be added to the beginning of sentence 8 to provide a better transition to the third paragraph (sentences 8–11)?

options.B: In contrast,
options.C: Meanwhile,
options.D: In summary,

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the transition that best connects the second paragraph (Enceladus) to the third paragraph (Cassini’s other work).

“Therefore,” is incorrect. It signals a cause and effect, but the discoveries at Enceladus did not cause Cassini to study Saturn’s rings and storms.
“In contrast,” is incorrect. It signals an opposite idea, but studying the rings and other moons does not contrast with studying Enceladus; both are part of the same mission.
“Meanwhile,” is correct. While the Enceladus discoveries described in paragraph 2 were happening, Cassini was also gathering data about the rings, storms, and other moons. “Meanwhile” shows that these things happened during the same period.
“In summary,” is incorrect. It signals a conclusion, but paragraph 3 adds new information rather than summing up the passage.

questions.question: Which revision of sentence 11 **best** maintains the formal style established in the passage?

options.A: However, by 2017, the spacecraft’s fuel tanks were running on fumes, leaving the mission in a real jam.
options.B: However, by 2017, the spacecraft’s fuel supply was nearly exhausted, placing the mission’s future in doubt.
options.C: However, by 2017, the spacecraft’s dwindling fuel cast a dark and ominous shadow over the fate of the mission.
options.D: However, by 2017, the spacecraft had pretty much burned through its fuel, which left the mission’s future up in the air.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks which revision best keeps the passage’s formal, factual style.

A. Incorrect. “Running on fumes” and “in a real jam” are casual, conversational expressions.
B. CORRECT. “Fuel supply was nearly exhausted” and “placing the mission’s future in doubt” are precise and formal, matching the rest of the passage.
C. Incorrect. “Cast a dark and ominous shadow over the fate” is overly dramatic; the passage reports facts without this kind of emotional language.
D. Incorrect. “Pretty much burned through” and “up in the air” are informal expressions.

questions.question:
Read this sentence.

**One of Cassini’s most exciting discoveries was evidence that a hidden ocean may lie beneath the icy surface of a moon.**

Where should the sentence be added to the passage?

options.B: between sentences 5 and 6
options.C: at the beginning of the second paragraph (before sentence 4)
options.D: between sentences 9 and 10

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks where the new sentence fits best.

A. Incorrect. Sentences 2 and 3 describe the mission’s purpose and length. A sentence about a hidden ocean would interrupt that introduction before the reader learns anything about Enceladus.
B. Incorrect. Sentences 5 and 6 describe the cracks and their nickname. Placing the sentence here would mention the ocean before the passage explains the jets that suggested it.
C. CORRECT. The second paragraph is about Enceladus and the evidence of an ocean under its ice. The new sentence works as a topic sentence that introduces this discovery, and sentences 4–7 then give the details.
D. Incorrect. Sentences 9 and 10 are about Cassini’s orbits and the Huygens probe on Titan, which have nothing to do with the hidden ocean.

questions.question: What is the **best** way to combine sentences 12 and 13?

options.A: Using up much of the spacecraft’s fuel, the team had regularly fired Cassini’s thrusters to steer it safely past Saturn’s moons prior to this fuel shortage.
options.B: Prior to this fuel shortage, the team had regularly fired Cassini’s thrusters to steer it safely past Saturn’s moons, using up much of the spacecraft’s fuel.
options.C: Regularly firing Cassini’s thrusters to steer it safely past Saturn’s moons prior to this fuel shortage, much of the spacecraft’s fuel had been used up by the team.
options.D: The team, prior to this fuel shortage, used up much of the spacecraft’s fuel because they had regularly fired Cassini’s thrusters to steer it safely past Saturn’s moons.

solution.exhibit_text:
The question asks for the clearest way to combine the two sentences.

A. Incorrect. The phrase “prior to this fuel shortage” connects back to sentence 11, so it works best at the beginning of the sentence. Here it is pushed to the end, and the opening phrase confusingly makes it sound as if the fuel was used up before the thrusters were fired.
B. CORRECT. The sentence keeps the transition “Prior to this fuel shortage” at the start, states what the team did, and then adds the result (“using up much of the spacecraft’s fuel”) in a clear phrase at the end.
C. Incorrect. The opening phrase “Regularly firing Cassini’s thrusters…” is a dangling modifier. It should describe the team, but the subject that follows is “much of the spacecraft’s fuel,” which could not fire anything.
D. Incorrect. Placing “prior to this fuel shortage” in the middle interrupts the sentence, and the result (using up fuel) is stated before its cause, which makes the order of events harder to follow.

grammar_questions.stimulus: In 1937 the Golden Gate Bridge opened to traffic in San <u>Francisco. At</u> the time, it was the longest suspension bridge in the world. Its famous orange color, officially called International <u>Orange, was</u> chosen partly because it stands out in the region’s thick <u>fog, the</u> color also blends well with the hills around the bay. Each of the bridge’s two main <u>cables, containing</u> more than 27,000 wires, is strong enough to support the enormous weight of the roadway.
grammar_questions.question:
Which part of the paragraph contains an error in sentence structure?

Select the one error.

options.B: Orange, was
options.C: fog, the
options.D: cables, containing

grammar_questions.solution:
**Concept: comma splices.** An independent clause has a subject and a verb and can stand alone as a sentence. Two independent clauses cannot be joined with only a comma; that mistake is called a comma splice. Fix it with a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a conjunction such as and, but, or so.

A. Correct as written. A period separates two complete sentences: “In 1937 the Golden Gate Bridge opened to traffic in San Francisco” and “At the time, it was the longest suspension bridge in the world.”
B. Correct as written. “Officially called International Orange” is extra information set off by a pair of commas, and “was” continues the main sentence (“Its famous orange color … was chosen”).
C. ERROR. “Its famous orange color … was chosen partly because it stands out in the region’s thick fog” and “the color also blends well with the hills around the bay” are both independent clauses, so joining them with only a comma creates a comma splice. Correct it with a period (“fog. The”) or “fog, and the.”
D. Correct as written. “Containing more than 27,000 wires” is a descriptive phrase set off by a pair of commas, and the main sentence continues with “is strong enough.”

grammar_questions.stimulus:
(1) The Mariana Trench is the deepest known place in the ocean.
(2) The Mariana Trench reaches nearly 36,000 feet below the surface.
grammar_questions.question:
Read these sentences.

What is the **best** way to combine the sentences to clarify the relationship between the ideas?

options.A: While the Mariana Trench is the deepest known place in the ocean, it reaches nearly 36,000 feet below the surface.
options.B: The Mariana Trench, which reaches nearly 36,000 feet below the surface, is the deepest known place in the ocean.
options.C: Although it reaches nearly 36,000 feet below the surface, the Mariana Trench is the deepest known place in the ocean.
options.D: The Mariana Trench is the deepest known place in the ocean, but it reaches nearly 36,000 feet below the surface.

grammar_questions.solution:
**Concept: showing how two ideas relate.** When you combine sentences, the connecting word has to match the real relationship between the ideas. “Although” and “but” signal a contrast, and “while” can signal a contrast or two things happening at the same time. When one sentence simply adds detail about a noun in the other, a relative clause (“which …”) is usually the clearest choice.

A. Incorrect. “While” suggests a contrast or a time relationship, but the depth does not contrast with being the deepest place; it explains it.
B. CORRECT. The clause “which reaches nearly 36,000 feet below the surface” adds a supporting detail about the trench, and the main clause keeps the key idea that it is the deepest known place.
C. Incorrect. “Although” signals a contrast that does not exist, since reaching 36,000 feet down is the reason the trench is the deepest place.
D. Incorrect. “But” also signals a contrast, which misstates how the two ideas are related.

grammar_questions.stimulus: (1) On the afternoon of August 14, 2003, a massive power outage struck large parts of the northeastern United States and Canada.  (2) Traffic lights went dark, trains stopped in their tunnels, and air conditioners fell silent.  (3) Trapped in elevators and subway cars for hours, the outage left thousands of commuters waiting to be rescued.  (4) The blackout, which affected about 50 million people, was one of the largest in North American history.
grammar_questions.question:
Which sentence in the paragraph contains an error in construction and should be revised?

There is only one error in construction.

options.B: Sentence 2
options.C: Sentence 3
options.D: Sentence 4

grammar_questions.solution:
**Concept: dangling modifiers.** A modifier is a phrase that describes something. An opening phrase such as “Trapped in elevators…” must be followed right away by the noun it describes. If a different noun comes next, the modifier is dangling, and the sentence seems to say something illogical.

Sentence 1: Construction is correct. The opening phrase tells when the outage happened, and the subject (“a massive power outage”) and verb (“struck”) are clear.
Sentence 2: Construction is correct. Three complete clauses are listed in parallel form, separated by commas, with “and” before the last one.
Sentence 3: Contains an error. “Trapped in elevators and subway cars for hours” should describe the commuters, but the noun right after the comma is “the outage,” so the sentence says the outage was trapped in elevators. A correct revision: “Trapped in elevators and subway cars for hours, thousands of commuters waited to be rescued.”
Sentence 4: Construction is correct. “Which affected about 50 million people” is a clause set off by commas that describes “the blackout.”

grammar_questions.stimulus: (1) Marcus <u>spent</u> the whole weekend building a model of a <u>volcano</u> for the science fair.  (2) First he <u>shapes</u> the cone out of <u>clay,</u> and newspaper so that it would be sturdy enough to stand on its own.  (3) Then he <u>painted</u> the sides brown and gray to make its ridges and <u>valleys</u> look realistic.  (4) Finally he <u>tested</u> the eruption in his backyard several <u>times,</u> adjusting the amounts of baking soda and vinegar each time.
grammar_questions.question: How should the paragraph be revised?

options.A: Sentence 1: Change **spent** to **had spent**, AND insert a comma after **volcano**.
options.B: Sentence 2: Change **shapes** to **shaped**, AND delete the comma after **clay**.
options.C: Sentence 3: Change **painted** to **paints**, AND insert a comma after **valleys**.
options.D: Sentence 4: Change **tested** to **tests**, AND delete the comma after **times**.

grammar_questions.solution:
**Concept: consistent verb tense and unnecessary commas.** A paragraph that tells about past events should stay in the past tense unless there is a reason to change. Also, do not put a comma between just two items joined by “and” (“clay and newspaper”), because a comma there splits a single compound object.

A. Incorrect. “Spent” is already in the past tense like the rest of the paragraph, and no comma belongs between “volcano” and “for the science fair.”
B. CORRECT. “Shapes” is present tense, but every other verb (“spent,” “painted,” “tested”) is past tense, so it should be “shaped.” The comma after “clay” wrongly separates the two parts of “clay and newspaper.”
C. Incorrect. “Painted” correctly matches the past tense, and a comma after “valleys” would wrongly separate the subject “ridges and valleys” from “look.”
D. Incorrect. “Tested” is correct, and the comma after “times” correctly sets off the phrase “adjusting the amounts …”
